# Draft:Kingdom of Italy–Ottoman relations

Unknown|envoy2= Ahmet Rüstem Bey}}
Following the revolts of 1820–21, the Ottoman Empire sought closer relations with the House of Savoy, with Britain acting as an intermediary. British diplomat Sir Robert Liston encouraged Sultan Mahmud II to conclude a commercial treaty with the Kingdom of Sardinia, negotiations for which began in 1820 and resulted in an agreement signed in 1823. This treaty reflected Britain’s wider free-trade strategy and the shared Ottoman and British interest in limiting French influence in Mediterranean commerce.
During the mid-19th century, the Ottoman Empire generally maintained neutrality in the conflicts associated with Italian unification, including the wars between Sardinia and Austria. Ottoman diplomats closely monitored Piedmontese mobilization in 1859, viewing war as increasingly unavoidable, and formally declared neutrality once hostilities began. In 1861, the Ottoman Empire recognized the newly proclaimed Kingdom of Italy, though celebrations in Istanbul were discouraged in order to avoid provoking Austria.
After Italy completed its unification with the capture of Rome in 1870, its growing industrial strength and expanding diplomatic ambitions gradually altered relations with the Ottoman Empire. Italy’s alignment with the Triple Alliance in 1882 and its pursuit of imperial expansion in North Africa increased competition over Ottoman territories, particularly Libya. These tensions culminated in the Italo-Turkish War of 1911–1912, in which Italy seized Ottoman Tripolitania and Cyrenaica and occupied the Dodecanese islands.
At the outbreak of World War I, both Italy and the Ottoman Empire were initially neutral, but they entered opposing alliances: the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in late 1914, while Italy entered the Entente in 1915 and formally declared war on the Ottoman Empire in August of that year.
History
Ottomans and Italian Unification
Following the Revolts of 1820-21, the Ottoman Empire attempted to form closer relations with the House of Savoy. The British were the middlemen between the Ottomans and the Kingdom of Sardinia, with Sir Robert Liston acting as a key figure in motivating both parties to cooperate. Lists personally encouraged Sultan Mahmud II to enter into a commercial treaty with Sardinia in 1820, and the Sultan indicated that he would be willing, leading to the commencement of negotiations shortly thereafter. Although Liston did not complete his term before this process was complete, the British continued to provide support for the process by naming Liston’s successor to continue negotiating. The treaty was signed in late 1823. The treaty exemplified the broader free trade strategy of Britain, as well as showing that the Ottomans were interested in strengthening ties with the Northern Italian states. Additionally, both Britain and the Ottomans viewed trade with Sardinia as one method of limiting French influence on trade in the Mediterranean.
Although the Ottoman Empire maintained neutrality in the war between Sardinia and Austria and the Italian Independence War of 1848, the Ottoman ambassador to Vienna congratulated Emperor Ferdinand of Austria, who returned to Vienna after the Battle of Custoza and expressed good intentions.The Ottoman Empire closely observed the mobilization efforts of Piedmont in early 1859, believing them to be an indication that they are preparing for war with Austria. Diplomats in the Ottoman Empire were reporting that volunteers were being recruited and there was anti-Austrian agitation from within the Ottoman Empire, all of which made the Ottomans to look for a way to obtain Britain's opinion on whether or not diplomacy or a Congress could help to end the war before it started. With the ultimatum issued by Austria, the Ottomans felt that war was now inevitable.
Once hostilities began, the Ottomans attempted to stay neutral (while keeping the peace) and trying to keep from creating unrest in the Balkans. After Britain issued a neutral statement on 5 May 1859, the Ottomans also declared themselves to be neutrals in order to continue their balance-of-power system and refrain from involvement in the conflict between France and Austria. The Ottoman Empire exercised caution during the period of the unification of Italy with regard to the reactions of the rest of Europe. Reports from Ottoman envoys indicated that Britain would support the recognition of the Kingdom of Italy, while the entire British government viewed Victor Emmanuel II as the King of Italy. On 30 July 1861, the Ottoman Empire formally recognised the Kingdom of Italy but discouraged celebrations in Istanbul to avoid upsetting Austria.
]]
Kingdom of Italy and Ottoman Empire
The announcement of The Italian Kingdom became one of the significant changes in history, both for the Italians and for their dealings with the Ottoman Empire. Upon the successful takeover of Rome on 20 September 1870, it became apparent, to the leaders of Italy, that the time for Italy to emerge as a nation-state of strength and power to compete with other nations would soon arrive. As a result of these actions, Italy started building itself to be a player in influencing both the balance of power in the Mediterranean and also in the Balkans.
Italy began with an effort to establish cordial relations and neutrality with the Ottoman Empire. However, following Italy's industrial advances in the 1870s and enhanced Italian involvement in European diplomacy in the 1880s, Italy began a significant transformation of its foreign affairs. This transformation had as one of its steps the signing of the Triple Alliance agreement in Vienna between Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy on 20 May 1882 and the desire of Italy for establishing Italy as a power in the world through imperial expansion in Africa. Although the French and the British were the dominant powers in North Africa, the British agreed to support Italy's interests in North Africa by way of an agreement concluded on 12 February 1887. Following this agreement, Italy began pursuing its interests through diplomatic relations with the major European powers, and the Ottoman Empire increasingly became the focus of the competition between European nations as they sought empire in North Africa.
Italo-Turkish War
Starting from the late 19th century, Italy had a territorial claim over Ottoman Libya. This claim dated back to the Ottoman Empire's defeat by Russia during the war of 1877–1878 and subsequent discussions after the Congress of Berlin in 1878, in which France and the United Kingdom had agreed to the French occupation of Tunisia and British control over Cyprus respectively, which were both parts of the declining Ottoman Empire. When Italian diplomats hinted about possible opposition by their government, the French replied that Tripoli would have been a counterpart for Italy, which made a secret agreement with the British government in February 1887 via a diplomatic exchange of notes.The agreement stipulated that Italy would support British control in Egypt, and that Britain would likewise support Italian influence in Libya.
In 1902, a diplomatic crisis between Italy and the Ottoman Empire took place. The crisis began due to the Ottomans failing to prevent attacks by Turkish Arabs on Italian sambuks. When the Ottoman Empire refused to take precautions to prevent these attacks after repeated Italian threats, Italian warships bombarded Port Midi from 31 October onwards. On 10 November, the Ottoman Empire capitulated and agreed to take measures to curb piracy as well as pay an indemnity, ending the crisis.

During the conflict, Italian forces also occupied the Dodecanese islands in the Aegean Sea. Italy agreed to return the Dodecanese to the Ottoman Empire in the Treaty of Ouchy in 1912. However, the vagueness of the text, combined with subsequent adverse events unfavourable to the Ottoman Empire (the outbreak of the Balkan Wars and World War I), allowed a provisional Italian administration of the islands, and Turkey eventually renounced all claims on these islands in Article 15 of the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne.

Though both states were initially neutral during World War I, the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in November 1914 and Italy joined the Entente in May 1915; Italy officially declared war on the Ottoman Empire on 21 August 1915.
